title: Do Less to Do More
author: Chris Martin
summary: Chris Martin's essay draws on Cal Newport's Slow Productivity to argue that modern work culture mistakes busyness for productivity, and that the solution is not better time management but a principled reduction in the number of tasks one undertakes simultaneously. Martin frames productivity as a stewardship question: those called to work are called to steward their vocational capacity well, which means refusing the false abundance of perpetual availability and task accumulation. The essay traces how pseudo-productivity -- doing many things poorly -- has become the default because it is visible, measurable, and socially rewarded even when it produces little of value. Newport's prescription is radical reduction: concentrate on fewer things, work at a natural pace, and produce outputs that actually matter. Martin contextualizes this for readers who may find pure productivity framing alien, showing how theological stewardship and Newport's practical wisdom converge.
points: * Modern work culture conflates busyness with productivity; the visible accumulation of tasks creates the appearance of performance without the substance. * Slow Productivity's core prescription is radical reduction: doing fewer things simultaneously, working at a natural pace, and resisting the culture of perpetual availability. * Productivity is a stewardship question: we are called to care for our vocational capacity, which means refusing to squander it on tasks that do not actually matter. * The problem is not that workers lack discipline; it is that organizational incentive structures reward visible busyness rather than substantive output. * Whether from secular or Christian wisdom traditions, the call converges: do less, do it well, do it sustainably.
quotes: This is my second in what will be a series of posts reflecting on various themes on work and productivity I've picked out of Cal Newport's book Slow Productivity.
But before we get into the meat here, let me address something.
Maybe you're reading this and you're like, "Why does this guy who writes devotional reflections or essays about social media care about productivity and work culture stuff?" Fair question.
Let me do my best to answer this if it's bubbling up for you.
Like I will say in the article below: we only have one life to live, and many of us will spend much of this life working.
Because of that reality, if nothing else, we should take our work seriously!

Not all of us work traditional jobs--some of us are keeping homes running, ferrying kids around town, and doing other kinds of work that doesn't result in a paycheck--but for those of us who have careers, we are called to steward those careers well!
